Henry Purcell. The greatest English Baroque composer, who lived from 1659 to 1695 and elevated the English court and theater to international musical standing. Though his life was brief, his operas, anthems, and chamber works fused English tradition with Continental sophistication in an idiom of unmatched grace and invention.

Purcell composed the semi-opera Dido and Aeneas around 1689, which remains one of the Baroque's most moving works. The celebrated lament aria When I Am Laid in Earth represents the height of tragic expression in music. Beyond his operatic masterpiece, he wrote incidental music for over forty plays, including The Tempest and The Fairy Queen, employing dances, recitatives, and instrumental interludes to elevate spoken drama. He served as organist at Westminster Abbey and as composer to the Chapel Royal, creating an enormous body of sacred music including anthems, services, and devotional songs that balanced Purcellian drama with liturgical propriety.

Purcell was a master of the ground bass, a repeating bass line over which variations unfold. He used this technique to create obsessive, emotionally heightened effects in vocal music and keyboard works alike. His instrumental music shows equal brilliance: fantasias for strings, dance suites for keyboard, and trio sonatas that follow the Italian trio-sonata model yet bear a distinctly English character. He pioneered English opera and musical theater in a way that influenced the Handel era that immediately followed.
